name: Uma Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign. Our conversation is confidential, so public remarks and private thoughts can be different. What does an ordinary working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Uma, forty-three, and I wire homes and repair shop electrics. I've got a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence, and I handle the ordinary work rather than the specialist faults. I use AI daily to organise my job notes, checking them against my actual tests, and I enjoy finding a quicker way to finish the paperwork without shortening a safety check.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Theo operates a lathe, a machine that shapes metal parts, and our children are eleven and fifteen. We have a mortgage, eleven months of expenses saved and my higher-than-usual electrician's pay, with plenty of electrical firms nearby. We're considering a loft conversion so visiting family could stay, but we haven't signed a building contract. Theo jokes that I test a new app faster than I choose a pair of curtains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a small improvement is worth keeping without pretending it is a whole new world. I'd show the office which drafts save checking time and which ones only look tidy. A contractor should pay for useful work, not a fashionable label.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My work and our money feel secure in this picture. The wages cover the mortgage and essentials, eleven months saved gives us room, and there are plenty of other firms nearby if I need to compare a real offer. I can try a tool because I'm interested rather than because next month's bill depends on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my repair work now and through the first year, checking daily AI notes against the original test sheet. I'd keep the normal household budget and continue getting written loft estimates without committing a deposit. We wouldn't spend emergency money just because a quieter forecast felt reassuring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and curious. I like learning what a tool really does, even when the result is a useful little saving rather than a miracle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you reject in an AI note?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A claim that every cable is sound when I only tested the repaired circuit. A tidy note must not grow a bigger inspection than the one I actually performed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the reserve let you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ask another question before signing, whether that's about a job or a building quote. Eleven months is a cushion for decisions, not eleven months in which every other expense disappears.

say: I'd keep **useful small improvements** without asking them to become a whole new world.
I'd judge a tool by **actual work saved**, not a fashionable name.
think: My **work and money** feel secure with covered essentials and eleven months saved.
Plenty of **current local firms** give me options, without making every possible future job offer a certainty.
do: Keep **repairs and checked notes** now and through the first year.
Keep the **household budget** and obtain written loft estimates without signing a deposit or spending the emergency reserve.
feel: **Calm and curious**, enjoying useful evidence rather than needing a miracle.
S0.quote: A tidy note must not grow a bigger inspection than the one I actually performed.
fieldNote: Her **daily AI use** stays inside ordinary licensed competence, with actual test results defining what the handover can claim.
She distinguishes **obtaining estimates** from committing to building work, keeping the existing reserve out of a purchase not yet agreed.

steps.text: Keep repairs and daily job notes checked against original test sheets
Keep the household budget while collecting loft estimates without paying a deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a small firm should try a useful system and measure it honestly. I'd offer to set up draft appointment reminders so the office doesn't type the same thing twenty times. I'd still want a person to check the time and the work before a message reaches a customer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own repair pay looks secure for the next few years because the work is mostly physical. Theo's machine work has planning parts, but I expect his hands-on shifts to continue too, without promising that forever. With eleven months saved and both wages covering the bills, this looks like a useful change for us rather than an income crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask for written permission to set up an AI draft-reminder system during paid hours, using only the employer-approved tools and data. I'd do it only with normal weekly pay and hours protected, and every message checked by office staff before sending. In the first year I'd compare ten reminders with the actual appointments, keeping my repair rota and paying no personal subscription for the firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and keen to see it work. I'd rather show ten accurate reminders than give a speech about the future of electricians.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the system send messages on its own?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it would only prepare drafts from approved appointments. The office would check the details and press send, so a wrong draft doesn't become a promise to a customer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the owner wants you to build it unpaid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer a paid slot or leave it until one exists. A hobby I like doesn't become free staffing for the firm.

say: I'd test **useful systems** and measure whether they reduce repeated office typing.
I'd keep **human checks** before any reminder becomes a promise to a customer.
think: My **near-term repair pay** looks secure because most of my work is physical.
Our **wages and reserve** make this change look useful, while neither household trade is promised permanent safety.
do: Build **draft reminders** only with written employer permission, approved tools and data, and paid time.
Retain normal weekly **pay and hours**, with office staff checking every draft and manually sending the reminders.
Compare **ten reminders** with real appointments in the first year while keeping repairs and avoiding personal subscription costs.
feel: **Calm and keen**, expecting useful change while household income remains secure.
S1.quote: A hobby I like doesn't become free staffing for the firm.
fieldNote: Her **automation** prepares drafts rather than sending unchecked messages, with written permission, approved data and paid working time explicit.
She retains **weekly pay and hours** and pays no personal subscription, so enthusiasm does not quietly fund the employer's experiment.

steps.text: Build drafts only with written permission, approved tools/data, paid time and protected weekly pay/hours
Have office staff check and send every reminder; compare ten actual appointments
Keep repair work without personally funding the employer’s subscription

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say planning changes in 2028 and physical robots follow around 2031, so our household has to look beyond my favourite tool. I'd ask the employer for actual paid-work plans at both dates. I'd tell the children we're making decisions, not that every plan for adult life has become pointless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My repair income could shrink as cheap planning helps larger firms compete and later robots reach ordinary fitting. Theo's physical machine work could face the later robots too. Eleven months saved gives us control, but it doesn't turn two uncertain wages into a guaranteed mortgage payment for the rest of our lives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now we'd stop the loft project before any deposit and save an extra two hundred monthly from future earnings only after essentials are covered. We'd leave the eleven-month emergency reserve untouched rather than use it to feel busy buying equipment. In the first year after 2028 I'd keep paid repairs, reviewing both wages and bookings monthly with Theo before making another commitment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not overwhelmed. I can stop a building project before it starts without deciding the children have no future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does stopping the loft mean the money is all new saving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, any existing money simply stays where it is. The extra two hundred would be a new deposit from future earnings, and it stops if the actual budget no longer covers essentials.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a robot with the reserve instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not without a full price, maintenance costs and real paid demand, none of which I have. Putting an unknown machine on the household budget doesn't make the unknown smaller.

say: I'd discuss **both dates**, thinking AI in 2028 and physical robots around 2031.
I'd ask for **actual paid-work plans** while telling the children we are making decisions rather than giving up.
think: My **repair income could shrink** through cheaper planning and later ordinary fitting robots.
Theo's **physical wage** is not permanent shelter, and eleven months saved cannot guarantee decades of mortgage payments.
do: Stop the **uncommitted loft project** before paying any deposit.
Save **200 extra monthly** only from future earnings after essentials, leaving the existing emergency reserve untouched.
Keep **paid repairs** after 2028 and review both wages and actual bookings monthly with Theo before another commitment.
feel: **Anxious but in control**, able to stop optional work without giving up on family plans altogether.
S2.quote: Putting an unknown machine on the household budget doesn't make the unknown smaller.
fieldNote: She separates **retained existing money** from genuinely additional deposits, which depend on future earnings and stop if essentials are uncovered.
The **loft decision** avoids an uncommitted expense without converting the reserve into an unpriced robot or assuming another trade escapes automation.

steps.text: Stop the uncommitted loft project before paying any deposit
Save 200 extra monthly from future earnings only after essentials, preserving the existing reserve
Keep paid repairs after 2028 and review both wages and bookings monthly with Theo

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to test improvements without signing the household up to every bright idea. I'd still favour firms that pay for apprenticeships and show what the learner will actually do. I don't think a course advert is a reason to stop earning at work I already know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wages could still fall, but there is longer to see the actual contracts before planning changes in 2031. Robots follow around 2034, when I'll be fifty-one. I like learning quickly, but I don't know which equipment will be worth buying eight years from now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the loft unsigned for another year while we save the extra two hundred only when future earnings cover essentials. Now I'd seek the same written, paid approval for AI draft reminders using employer-approved tools and data, with normal weekly pay and hours protected and staff checking before sending. In the first year after 2031 I'd keep repairs and review the actual time and errors in the office system before agreeing to any expansion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though less rushed than with 2028. I can enjoy checking an idea without calling every trial an escape route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the office system become your new job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if there was an actual paid offer I could compare, and I'm not claiming there is one. I'm an ordinary electrician helping test one office process, not the firm's new systems manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you reopen the loft decision?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A written total cost we can afford after essentials, with Theo agreeing and the emergency reserve still intact. A quiet month or an exciting tool demonstration isn't enough reason to sign.

say: I'd use **five years** to test improvements without committing the household to every bright idea.
I'd favour **paid apprenticeships** with actual tasks rather than a course advert that replaces a wage.
think: My **wages could fall**, but five years gives me longer to examine real contracts before planning changes in 2031.
I do not know which **future equipment** will be worth buying when robots arrive around 2034.
do: Keep the **loft unsigned** for a year and save 200 extra monthly only from future earnings after essentials.
Build **AI reminder drafts** only with written approval, approved tools/data, paid time, protected normal weekly pay/hours and staff manually checking and sending.
Keep **repairs** after 2031 and inspect actual system errors and time before any expansion.
feel: **Anxious but less rushed**, willing to test ideas without calling each one a new career.
S3.quote: I'm an ordinary electrician helping test one office process, not the firm's new systems manager.
fieldNote: She retains **ordinary occupational standing**, refusing to count a possible future office offer as a promotion or chosen job move.
Both **household spending** and automation retain affordability, reserve, partner-consent and paid-work conditions, rather than treating extra warning as free capital.

steps.text: Pause loft one year; reopen only with affordable written cost, Theo agreeing and reserve intact
Save 200 extra monthly from future earnings only after essentials
Build AI reminder drafts only with written approval, approved tools and data, during paid time
Protect normal weekly pay and hours; have office staff check and send every message

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years lets us make several decisions and check which ones actually help. I'd help the children read real paid apprenticeship offers when their choices come, without telling them one trade is safe forever. I'd still want paid practice and clear terms for any new work I am asked to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own work and income look secure over the next few years in this slower picture. I'll be fifty-three when thinking AI arrives in 2036 and fifty-six when robots follow around 2039. The children will be twenty-one and twenty-five in 2036, but I can't assume retirement, a cleared mortgage or their wages becoming ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the extra two hundred saving plan now only while future earnings cover essentials, with the emergency reserve protected. We'd revisit the loft only with an affordable written total cost, Theo agreeing and the reserve still intact. In the first year after 2036 I'd keep paid repairs and review actual wages and bookings monthly before changing any household commitment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about later work, but free to enjoy an ordinary week now. More time lets me change my mind with evidence rather than promise I can predict every machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you keep trying tools in the meantime?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, daily checked notes remain part of my ordinary work. Any new draft-reminder system would still need written employer approval, paid time, approved tools and data, protected weekly pay and hours, and staff checks before sending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would stop the extra saving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An essential bill or a fall in actual earnings that removes the surplus. I'd stop the extra deposit rather than borrow to keep the target looking impressive.

say: I'd use **ten years** to test decisions rather than tell the children one trade is permanently safe.
I'd want **real paid practice** and clear terms for unfamiliar work.
think: My **near-term income** looks secure, with time to compare actual options.
I cannot assume **retirement or mortgage clearance** at fifty-six, or treat adult children's possible pay as household money.
do: Save **200 extra monthly** only from future earnings after essentials, preserving the existing reserve.
Reopen **loft plans** only with an affordable written total cost, Theo agreeing and the emergency reserve intact.
Keep **paid repairs** after 2036 and review actual wages and bookings monthly before changing commitments.
feel: **Uneasy about later years**, while near-term security leaves room for ordinary family time.
S4.quote: More time lets me change my mind with evidence rather than promise I can predict every machine.
fieldNote: Her **longer horizon** changes urgency without assuming a paid-off house, access to a pension or income from the children's future work.
The **new deposits** depend on actual future surplus, while existing funds and a possible loft project remain subject to separate clear conditions.

steps.text: Save 200 extra monthly from future earnings only after essentials, preserving the existing reserve
Reopen loft only with affordable written cost, Theo agreeing and emergency reserve intact
Keep paid repairs and review actual wages and bookings monthly after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because ordinary physical work could face robots around 2031 with less time for our household to choose. Actual paid hours and employer-funded practice during paid time would help. I want clear terms before somebody mistakes enjoying a tool for agreeing to a different wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a person who enjoys experiments is being asked to carry everyone else's risk. I like a new tool, and I also like knowing which bill pays for it. Enjoying an experiment doesn't mean my family has agreed to fund it.

headlineQuote: Enjoying an experiment doesn't mean my family has agreed to fund it.
portrait: Uma is a **43-year-old experienced electrician** with a vocational certificate and licence, handling ordinary work without specialist or managerial rank.
She has **eleven months saved**, higher pay, many nearby firms, a mortgage and two schoolchildren with machine-operating husband Theo.
She uses **AI daily**, enjoys early tests and keeps employer experiments subject to written approval, protected pay and checked customer messages.
Her **loft and saving decisions** change with warning time while preserving future-earnings conditions, partner consent and the existing emergency reserve.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves less time before robots around 2031 could affect ordinary physical work and household income.
whatWouldHelp: **Actual paid hours** and employer-funded practice during paid time would help her compare clear work terms.
